text: [INTRO MUSIC]

speaker: NORA
text: Here's a question that sounds simple and isn't. How much should a law firm charge for a piece of work, before the work has started? Not after, when the hours are all logged and the bill is easy to add up. Before. When the client is asking for a fixed fee and the partner has to put a number on the table.

speaker: JAMES
text: And here's why it's getting harder. For a century the answer was, more or less, multiply the hours by the rate. But clients are pushing for fixed fees and capped fees, and now AI is changing how many hours a piece of work takes in the first place. If a task that took ten hours now takes two, what do you charge?

speaker: NORA
text: That's the question sitting at the centre of today's company. Welcome to Portfolio Deep Dives, the show where we take one company at a time, look at its business, its market, its challenges and where AI could take it next. I'm Nora.

speaker: JAMES
text: And I'm James. Our series follows the companies in the portfolio of Levine Leichtman Capital Partners, a private equity firm based in Beverly Hills. Today it's BigHand, a London-based software company that has spent three decades working inside law firms.

speaker: NORA
text: The usual note before we begin. Everything we discuss comes from public sources as of November 2026: company announcements, trade press, the private equity firm's own pages. When something is our opinion or an inference, we'll say so. And when a number comes from the company itself or from a vendor-sponsored survey, we'll flag that too.

speaker: JAMES
text: Which matters today, because a lot of the most interesting numbers in this story come from BigHand's own research.

speaker: NORA
text: So, James. BigHand. If someone has never heard of it, what's the one-sentence version?

speaker: JAMES
text: BigHand makes the software that helps law firms run the business side of practising law. Who does which piece of work, how documents and tasks move through the firm, how matters are priced and budgeted, and how partners see what's happening across the practice. It says it has about four thousand two hundred customers and roughly eight hundred and ten thousand users around the world.

speaker: NORA
text: And the reason it's interesting right now?

speaker: JAMES
text: Because in August 2026 it bought a small AI company called Ayora, which specialises in AI-driven matter pricing. That deal is a bet that the most valuable thing BigHand owns isn't any single product. It's the data about how legal work actually gets done, and what it costs.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's start with the company itself. Where did BigHand come from?

speaker: JAMES
text: BigHand started life in the mid nineteen-nineties as a voice and dictation company. Its own site says it was founded in 1996, and the private equity firm's page says 1995, so call it the mid-nineties. The original product was digital dictation for lawyers. If you've ever seen a partner dictating a letter for an assistant to type up, BigHand built the digital version of that workflow.

speaker: NORA
text: Which sounds a long way from AI pricing.

speaker: JAMES
text: It does, but the thread is actually consistent. Dictation is about work moving from a lawyer to someone who supports them. Once you're managing that handoff, you naturally get into task management, delegation, who's busy and who isn't. And once you know who is doing what, you're sitting on data about time and effort. Pricing is the next step along that chain.

speaker: NORA
text: So what does the product line look like today?

speaker: JAMES
text: BigHand lists around sixteen solutions, grouped into what it calls people, document and financial productivity. On the people side there's workflow and delegation, resource management, the tools that help a firm figure out which associate or support person should take on which task. On the document side there's document creation and automation. And on the financial side there's matter pricing and budgeting, time and billing analytics, and business intelligence for partners and finance teams.

speaker: NORA
text: Sixteen products is a lot.

speaker: JAMES
text: It is, and we'll come back to that, because it's both a strength and a weakness. Breadth means BigHand touches a lot of the firm. But many of those products came in through acquisitions, and stitching them into one coherent experience is real work.

speaker: NORA
text: Who are the customers?

speaker: JAMES
text: Law firms, overwhelmingly. BigHand's own figures say it works with eighty-seven percent of the UK Top 200 firms and seventy-two percent of the American Lawyer 200. I'd treat those as company claims, and we've seen slightly different percentages on different pages of its own site. But the direction is clear. This is a vendor with deep penetration into large, established law firms on both sides of the Atlantic.

speaker: NORA
text: Where is it based?

speaker: JAMES
text: Headquartered in London, with offices in Chicago, Seattle and Sydney. And the leadership team, according to its 2026 announcements, includes Sam Toulson as chief executive and Rob Stote as chief product officer. Stote led the Ayora deal, which tells you that the product organisation is driving the AI strategy.

speaker: NORA
text: And size?

speaker: JAMES
text: That's one of the gaps. Revenue isn't public. An older section of its website said more than three hundred and fifty employees, but that dates from around 2022, so it's stale. What we can say is that it has grown from three and a half thousand organisations and six hundred thousand users in 2020 to about four thousand two hundred customers and eight hundred and ten thousand users now, by its own count.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's do the ownership history, because I think it tells you a lot about the company's character.

speaker: JAMES
text: It's a classic British software private equity story. In 2006 the founders sold to a management buyout backed by LDC, which is the private equity arm of Lloyds Banking Group. In 2012, Bridgepoint Development Capital bought BigHand in a buyout reported at forty-eight million pounds. Then in August 2020, Levine Leichtman agreed to acquire BigHand from Bridgepoint, with LDC coming back as a minority co-investor and management rolling a stake.

speaker: NORA
text: So three private equity owners in about fourteen years.

speaker: JAMES
text: Three, and with real continuity in management. That pattern is common in vertical software. Each owner takes the business a stage further. The first buyout gives the founders liquidity. The second funds growth and professionalisation. The third, in this case, has been about broadening the product set and, more recently, AI.

speaker: NORA
text: And acquisitions under the current owner?

speaker: JAMES
text: A few. In late 2020 there was a consulting firm acquisition reported in the legal tech press. In February 2022 BigHand bought Iridium Technology from Polaris Growth Fund, which brought in Iridium's business intelligence tools, plus products called Intellistat, Steere and SmartTime. There was also Impact Analytics, formerly known as Digitory, a pricing and analytics business, although we couldn't pin down the date. And then in August 2026, Ayora.

speaker: NORA
text: How long has the current owner held it?

speaker: JAMES
text: The investment was in October 2020, so about six years as we record this. In private equity terms, that's a mature hold. Which means people will be asking what the next chapter looks like, and that's another reason the AI story matters so much. A buyer in a future sale will want to see AI that has actually shipped and is producing revenue, not just a strategy deck.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's talk about the customer problem. What's actually hard about running a law firm?

speaker: JAMES
text: More than outsiders think. A large law firm is essentially thousands of highly paid professionals selling their time, with a huge support operation behind them. The partners own the business, but most of them are lawyers first and managers second. And the economics depend on a few things that are surprisingly hard to measure. How much work is actually being done. How long things really take. Whether a matter is profitable. Whether the right person is doing the right task.

speaker: NORA
text: Give me an example.

speaker: JAMES
text: Take delegation. A partner needs a document drafted, a set of court papers prepared and a research memo written. In a lot of firms, that work gets handed out by email or by walking down the corridor. There's no central view of who's overloaded and who's free. Junior lawyers can be swamped while others are underused, and secretarial and support teams get tasks from ten directions at once. BigHand's workflow tools put structure around that. Tasks get logged, routed, tracked and reported.

speaker: NORA
text: And the pricing side?

speaker: JAMES
text: Pricing is the bigger prize. Clients have pushed back on open-ended hourly billing for years. General counsel want certainty. They ask for fixed fees, capped fees, phased budgets. Collectively these are called alternative fee arrangements, or AFAs. And when a firm agrees a fixed fee, the economic risk moves from the client to the firm. If the work takes longer than expected, the firm eats the cost.

speaker: NORA
text: So the firm needs to know how long similar work took in the past.

speaker: JAMES
text: Exactly. And here's the surprising part. Many firms don't know that very well. BigHand's own 2023 research found that only thirty-nine percent of firms could give clients matter-level time information. The data exists in time entries, but it's messy. Narratives are inconsistent, tasks aren't coded properly, matters are opened under the wrong categories.

speaker: NORA
text: Garbage in, garbage out.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's literally how Ayora pitched itself. Its argument was that firms' historic matter data is too messy for AI to use directly, so the first step is cleaning and enriching it. Only then can you build a reliable pricing model on top.

speaker: NORA
text: So BigHand's customer problem has two layers. Run the work better day to day, and price the work better up front.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's a good summary. And the two layers feed each other. Better workflow data makes better pricing possible. Better pricing makes the workflow data more valuable.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's go a bit deeper on the product. Walk me through how a firm might actually use BigHand.

speaker: JAMES
text: Picture a mid-sized commercial law firm. A partner lands a new deal for a client. On the workflow side, the partner or their assistant creates tasks in BigHand: draft this, review that, prepare these schedules. Those tasks get routed to the right team, whether that's a document production unit, a secretarial pool or a junior lawyer, based on capacity and skills. Everyone can see what's waiting, what's late and what's done.

speaker: NORA
text: And the support teams see the queue rather than a pile of emails.

speaker: JAMES
text: Right. And in November 2025 BigHand added something that's a nice illustration of practical AI. It's called AI Email Routing. Support teams often have a shared inbox where requests arrive in free text. "Can someone format this agreement by three o'clock." AI Email Routing reads those emails, works out what's being asked, creates the task and routes it to the right person. BigHand made it available to cloud customers without an extra licence fee.

speaker: NORA
text: That's a very unglamorous use of AI.

speaker: JAMES
text: And I love it for that reason. It saves time on something people do hundreds of times a day, the data is right there in the inbox, and the risk is low because a human still does the actual work. That's the profile of a good first AI feature.

speaker: NORA
text: What about pricing?

speaker: JAMES
text: On the pricing side, a partner preparing a fee proposal would open BigHand's matter pricing and budgeting tool. It helps them build a budget by phase and task, using historic matters as a reference. Back in 2023, BigHand added AI-enabled timecard analysis to that product, which looks at the free-text narratives on time entries and classifies the work, so you can see what actually happened on past matters even if the coding was poor.

speaker: NORA
text: And Ayora goes further.

speaker: JAMES
text: Ayora adds a data enrichment layer that cleans and structures historic matter data, plus what it calls an AI Pricing Agent that helps produce a price or budget. In May 2026 the two companies announced a partnership to integrate it into BigHand's Matter Pricing and Budgeting. In August BigHand bought Ayora outright. At the time of the acquisition, the integrated capability was described as coming "later this year", so as of our recording, we haven't seen evidence it's fully in customers' hands.

speaker: NORA
text: So the AI pricing story is partly shipped and partly still to come.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's the honest picture. Timecard analysis from 2023 and email routing from 2025 are shipped. The agentic pricing assistant is the big next step, and it's the one that matters most for the investment case.

speaker: NORA
text: Then there's business intelligence.

speaker: JAMES
text: Yes. The Iridium acquisition brought BI tools designed for law firms, so partners and finance teams can see utilisation, realisation, work in progress, how matters are tracking. In BigHand's 2026 framing, the shift is from backward-looking reporting to decisions made before and during a matter. Not just telling you that a matter overran, but warning you while there's still time to do something.

speaker: NORA
text: Before we get to competitors, I want to ask a broader question. In a world where general AI assistants can draft documents and summarise emails, why does a specialised legal software company still matter?
chapter: Why vertical software holds on in legal

speaker: JAMES
text: It's the question every vertical software company is being asked right now. My answer for legal has three parts. The first is workflow specificity. Law firms have very particular ways of working. Conflict checks, matter opening, delegation rules between partners and support teams, time recording in six-minute units, billing guidelines that differ by client. A general assistant doesn't know any of that out of the box. Specialist software encodes it.
chapter: Why vertical software holds on in legal

speaker: NORA
text: Second?
chapter: Why vertical software holds on in legal

speaker: JAMES
text: The second is the system of record. BigHand isn't just a tool people use, it's where the tasks, the time and the pricing history are stored. Whoever holds the record of how work was done is in the best position to apply AI to it. General assistants are brilliant at language, but they need data to reason about, and in a law firm that data lives in systems like BigHand's.
chapter: Why vertical software holds on in legal

speaker: NORA
text: And third?
chapter: Why vertical software holds on in legal

speaker: JAMES
text: The third is trust and accountability. When a law firm signs a contract with a specialist vendor, it gets a supplier that understands legal confidentiality obligations, has been through the firm's security review, and can be held to account. That matters a lot in a profession where a data mistake can end careers.
chapter: Why vertical software holds on in legal

speaker: NORA
text: So the general assistant becomes a front end, and the specialist system becomes the brain with the memory.
chapter: Why vertical software holds on in legal

speaker: JAMES
text: That's a nice way to put it. In fact, I'd expect the smart move for BigHand over time is to make its data and AI available inside the tools lawyers already use. If a partner lives in Outlook and Word, the pricing agent should be reachable from there. You don't fight the general assistant, you plug into it, and you bring the firm-specific data and logic it lacks.
chapter: Why vertical software holds on in legal

speaker: NORA
text: Is there a risk in that? Making yourself invisible?
chapter: Why vertical software holds on in legal

speaker: JAMES
text: There is, which is why the brand and the value need to be clear. But I think the bigger risk is the opposite: insisting that lawyers come to your application when the rest of their day is somewhere else. Adoption follows convenience.
chapter: Why vertical software holds on in legal

speaker: NORA
text: Let's talk market. How big is legal practice management software?

speaker: JAMES
text: I'm going to be careful, because we didn't find a reliable, current market size figure for BigHand's specific niche, and I don't want to quote a number we can't stand behind. What we can say is that legal technology overall has been one of the hottest areas for AI investment over the past couple of years, with a lot of venture money going into AI tools for legal research, drafting and review.

speaker: NORA
text: Who does BigHand compete with?

speaker: JAMES
text: It depends on the product line, which is part of the challenge of a sixteen-product suite. In broad practice management and financial systems, the big names in the industry are firms like Intapp, Aderant and Thomson Reuters with its Elite products, and Clio in the smaller-firm market. That's from general industry knowledge rather than anything BigHand says about itself. In document automation there are many specialists, some of which have been acquired by bigger platforms. And in pricing specifically, there's a wave of AI-native startups trying to do exactly what Ayora does.

speaker: NORA
text: And the horizontal threat.

speaker: JAMES
text: The horizontal threat is general-purpose AI. If every lawyer has Microsoft Copilot or a similar assistant in their email and documents, some of what BigHand does at the edges, triaging emails, drafting standard documents, could start to feel like a feature of the office suite rather than a separate product.

speaker: NORA
text: So what's BigHand's defence?

speaker: JAMES
text: Two things, in my view. First, depth in the specific workflows of law firms. A general assistant doesn't know your firm's delegation rules, your resourcing model or your pricing policies. Second, and more important, data. BigHand has years of time, task and matter data inside thousands of firms. That's very hard for a horizontal tool to replicate, and it's exactly what an AI pricing model needs.

speaker: NORA
text: Assuming firms let it be used that way.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's an important caveat. Law firms are very protective of their data, and for good reason. Any AI built on it has to respect confidentiality, client obligations and each firm's control over its own information. But within a single firm's own data, the opportunity is very real.

speaker: NORA
text: I want to spend some time on the big industry shift, because I think it's the key to this whole episode. How is AI changing the way law firms charge?

speaker: JAMES
text: It's genuinely unsettled. BigHand published a survey in September 2026 on pricing and budgeting trends. It was vendor-sponsored and we didn't see the sample size, so take it as directional. But the findings are fascinating. About twenty-nine percent of firms said they had changed how they price AI-augmented work. Fifty-three percent said clients would pay the same fee where AI improves outcomes. Twenty-six percent expected a premium, and seventeen percent expected clients to pay less.

speaker: NORA
text: So there's no consensus at all.

speaker: JAMES
text: None. And it gets more interesting. Thirty percent of firms said they keep AI efficiency gains internally, meaning they don't pass the savings on. Twenty-five percent offer discounts where clients permit AI. And when asked about barriers to discussing AI with clients, thirty-five percent cited partner discomfort and thirty-one percent regulatory concerns.

speaker: NORA
text: That's a market in the middle of a negotiation with itself.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's well put. And here's why it matters for BigHand. If billing stays purely hourly and AI reduces the hours, firms lose revenue unless they raise rates or change the model. If they move to fixed fees, they need very good data on what work really costs. Either way, the firms that understand their own matter economics will win, and the ones that don't will either leave money on the table or take on fixed fees that lose money.

speaker: NORA
text: So the shift actually increases demand for BigHand's pricing products.

speaker: JAMES
text: In the short to medium term, I think so. When the old pricing model is breaking, tools that help you build the new one become more valuable. That's the thesis behind the Ayora deal.

speaker: NORA
text: But there's a flip side.

speaker: JAMES
text: There is. A lot of BigHand's analytics value comes from timecards. If fixed fees and subscriptions eventually replace hourly billing for big chunks of work, lawyers may stop recording time in such detail. Then the time-based data asset becomes less rich over time. So BigHand needs to evolve from time data to work data, what was actually done, by whom, with what effort, whether or not it's billed by the hour.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's take stock of where BigHand actually is with AI right now. Strip out the marketing.

speaker: JAMES
text: Okay. Shipped and in customers' hands, as far as public evidence goes: AI-enabled timecard analysis in the pricing product, from 2023, and AI Email Routing for cloud customers, from November 2025. Bought and being integrated: Ayora's data enrichment and pricing agent, acquired August 2026. Stated intent: extending AI into resource management and business intelligence.

speaker: NORA
text: And who's leading it?

speaker: JAMES
text: The chief product officer, Rob Stote, is the visible face of the AI strategy. There are also signs of a dedicated AI and data products role, but we couldn't confirm the details from public sources. What we didn't find is a public AI governance page or a published approach to responsible AI, which for a company selling into law firms will become increasingly important.

speaker: NORA
text: Why law firms in particular?

speaker: JAMES
text: Because law firms will ask hard questions. Where does our data go? Is it used to train models for other firms? Can we explain how a price was generated if a client asks? Is the vendor certified for information security? Large firms run serious vendor security reviews. A clear, published AI governance stance can actually be a sales advantage.

speaker: NORA
text: So what's your overall read?

speaker: JAMES
text: BigHand is one of the more AI-advanced companies we'll cover in this series. It has real shipped features, a clear thesis and a deal to back it up. The gap is between the story and the revenue. The pricing agent needs to ship, work reliably on real firm data, and become something customers pay for.

speaker: NORA
text: We've talked a lot about software and data. Let's talk about people, because law firms are famously hard places to change.
chapter: People and change inside the firm

speaker: JAMES
text: They are. A law firm is a partnership. The partners are the owners, they're senior, they're busy, and they've been successful doing things their way. You can't mandate a new pricing tool the way a corporation might roll out a new system. You have to persuade.
chapter: People and change inside the firm

speaker: NORA
text: So who are the people BigHand has to win over?
chapter: People and change inside the firm

speaker: JAMES
text: I'd think about four groups. Partners, who make pricing decisions and own client relationships. Pricing and finance teams, who are often the internal champions for better data. Resource managers and support teams, who live in the workflow tools every day. And the associates and junior lawyers, whose time is being allocated and recorded.
chapter: People and change inside the firm

speaker: NORA
text: What does each of them care about?
chapter: People and change inside the firm

speaker: JAMES
text: Partners care about winning work and not losing money on it, and about not looking foolish in front of a client. If an AI tool helps them give a confident, defensible price faster, they'll use it. If it produces a number they can't explain, they won't. Pricing teams care about consistency and data quality. They're often the ones who know how messy the time data really is, so enrichment speaks directly to their pain.
chapter: People and change inside the firm

speaker: NORA
text: And the support teams?
chapter: People and change inside the firm

speaker: JAMES
text: They care about workload and fairness. AI routing that sends them clearer, better-organised tasks is a win. AI that's perceived as monitoring them is a risk. How the tools are introduced really matters.
chapter: People and change inside the firm

speaker: NORA
text: And associates?
chapter: People and change inside the firm

speaker: JAMES
text: Associates care about getting good work, developing their careers and not being buried. Smarter resource allocation can genuinely help them, if it's designed with them in mind. There's also a bigger question in the profession right now about how junior lawyers learn if AI does a lot of the routine work they used to cut their teeth on. That's not BigHand's problem to solve alone, but resource management tools will be part of the answer.
chapter: People and change inside the firm

speaker: NORA
text: So adoption is a change management project, not just a feature release.
chapter: People and change inside the firm

speaker: JAMES
text: Absolutely. The vendors that win in legal invest in customer success, training and champion programmes inside firms. BigHand's annual conference, which in 2026 included sessions on matter pricing with Ayora, is part of that. It's where firms share how they're using the tools, and peers convincing peers is very powerful in this market.
chapter: People and change inside the firm

speaker: NORA
text: You mentioned governance earlier. Let's dig in, because I think it's going to be one of the deciding factors in legal AI.

speaker: JAMES
text: I agree. Law firms hold some of the most sensitive information in the economy: deal terms before they're public, litigation strategy, personal data. They have strict duties of confidentiality to clients, and many clients put conditions on how their information can be used, including with AI.

speaker: NORA
text: So what does a firm want to know before it switches on an AI pricing agent?

speaker: JAMES
text: At least five things. Where the data is processed and stored. Whether the firm's data is used to train models that other firms benefit from. Which AI models are used underneath and under what terms. How outputs can be explained and audited. And what security certifications the vendor holds. On that last point, we couldn't independently confirm BigHand's certifications from public sources, so that's something a buyer would check directly.

speaker: NORA
text: And the training question seems especially important.

speaker: JAMES
text: It's the big one. The most valuable model in theory would learn across every firm's data. But firms will almost certainly insist that their data only improves their own pricing, not their competitors'. So the realistic design is firm-specific models or firm-specific enrichment on top of shared general capability. Any cross-firm benchmarking would need explicit consent and strong anonymisation.

speaker: NORA
text: Is there an upside to getting this right?

speaker: JAMES
text: A big one. A vendor that publishes a clear, strict AI and data policy, and can show it in security reviews, shortens sales cycles. In a market where firms are nervous, trust is a competitive advantage. I'd encourage BigHand to make its AI governance as visible as its AI features.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's be specific about the challenges. What keeps BigHand's leadership up at night, in your view?

speaker: JAMES
text: I'd name four. The first is integration and product sprawl. Sixteen products from at least seven acquisitions is a lot of different codebases, data models and user experiences. Every new AI feature is harder to deliver across a fragmented suite. The second is cloud migration. BigHand has said it is moving its portfolio to the cloud, which means there's still a legacy on-premise base. AI features like email routing are cloud-first, so the slower customers move, the slower the AI story reaches them.

speaker: NORA
text: Third?

speaker: JAMES
text: Proving Ayora. At the time of the deal, Ayora hadn't published named customers or metrics. That's normal for a small startup, but it means BigHand is buying a capability and a team, not a proven revenue line. The integration has to work in real firms with their real, messy data.

speaker: NORA
text: And fourth.

speaker: JAMES
text: Pricing BigHand's own AI. It's a bit meta. BigHand's customers are struggling to price AI-augmented work, and BigHand itself has to decide how to price AI features. Email routing was bundled for free for cloud customers, which is a sensible adoption play. But at some point, AI has to show up as revenue, whether through higher subscription tiers, premium pricing modules or new products.

speaker: NORA
text: You could say BigHand has to solve the same problem it's helping its customers solve.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's exactly right. How do you charge for the value AI creates, when AI is also reducing effort?

speaker: NORA
text: Okay, let's move to opportunities. If you were on BigHand's board, where would you push?

speaker: JAMES
text: The first and biggest is the obvious one: get the AI pricing agent live inside Matter Pricing and Budgeting, and sell it across the installed base. About four thousand two hundred customers, many of them large firms under pressure on AFAs. Even a modest share of them upgrading to an AI pricing tier would be meaningful.

speaker: NORA
text: How would you prioritise customers?

speaker: JAMES
text: I'd start with firms that already use BigHand's pricing product and already do a lot of fixed-fee work. They feel the pain, they have the data, and they can measure the result. The metric I'd care about is pricing accuracy. How close were budgets to actual costs before and after the AI. If BigHand can show firms that their fixed fees became more profitable, that's a very easy story to sell to managing partners.

speaker: NORA
text: What else?

speaker: JAMES
text: Second, agentic resource management. BigHand has said AI will extend to resource management. Imagine a system that looks at incoming work, skills, availability and deadlines, and proposes who should do what, with the resource manager approving. That saves resource managers hours, and it should improve utilisation and associate experience.

speaker: NORA
text: Third?

speaker: JAMES
text: Business intelligence that actually advises. Instead of a dashboard that shows a partner their matters, an assistant that says: these three matters are trending over budget, here's why, here's what similar matters did. That's the "decisions before and during the matter" idea made concrete.

speaker: NORA
text: And beyond the product?

speaker: JAMES
text: A fourth opportunity is benchmarking. BigHand runs an annual pricing and budgeting survey. With permission and proper anonymisation, aggregated insight across firms could become a paid benchmark product. Firms love to know how they compare to peers. I'd be cautious here, because data rights in law firms are sensitive. But it's worth exploring.

speaker: NORA
text: And North America?

speaker: JAMES
text: Yes, BigHand has stated a goal of growing in North America, and it already has offices in Chicago and Seattle. The AFA trend is strong in the US, and American firms are huge buyers of legal technology. An AI pricing product could be a strong wedge there.

speaker: NORA
text: And M&A?

speaker: JAMES
text: More bolt-ons are likely. BigHand has said it will make acquisitions where they make sense for customers. Natural targets would be more AI pricing or analytics capability, or document automation. But I'd say the priority should be integrating what it already owns before buying more.

speaker: NORA
text: If you had to pick one AI use case to bet the next eighteen months on, what is it?

speaker: JAMES
text: AI data enrichment plus a pricing agent inside Matter Pricing and Budgeting. It's the use case where BigHand has the strongest right to win. The data is already in its products. The Ayora team and technology are in-house. The market shift to AFAs creates demand. And the value is measurable in pricing accuracy and matter profitability.

speaker: NORA
text: How would you run it?

speaker: JAMES
text: I'd pick five to ten design partner firms with good historic data and real fixed-fee volume. Run the enrichment on their past matters, then use the agent to propose budgets for new matters alongside the partner's own estimate. Compare the two over a quarter. Where the agent was closer, show it. Where it was wrong, learn why. Only then roll it out more widely, with a clear price.

speaker: NORA
text: That's the shadow mode idea again.

speaker: JAMES
text: It is. In legal, it's essential. Partners will only trust an AI price if they've seen it be right on their own work. And they'll want to see the reasoning: these past matters, these phases, these adjustments. Explainability is not optional when you're putting a number in front of a general counsel.

speaker: NORA
text: And the second-best bet?

speaker: JAMES
text: Agentic resource management. It saves time for a specific, identifiable role, resource managers, and it improves something partners care about, which is getting the right people on the right work.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's make the pricing idea really concrete. Walk me through one fixed-fee proposal, today and with the AI pricing agent. An invented example, not a real firm.
chapter: A fixed-fee proposal, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Sure. Let's say a corporate partner at a large firm, call her Helen, is asked by a long-standing client for a fixed fee to run the legal work on a mid-sized acquisition. The client's general counsel wants one number by Friday, broken down by phase: due diligence, the purchase agreement, disclosure, completion.
chapter: A fixed-fee proposal, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: And how does Helen do that today?
chapter: A fixed-fee proposal, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: In a lot of firms, she does it from memory and a spreadsheet. She thinks about two or three similar deals she remembers. She asks finance to pull the time recorded on them. Finance sends back a report, but the time entries were coded inconsistently, so it's hard to tell how much went on diligence versus drafting. One of the deals had a messy negotiation that blew the budget, another was unusually smooth. Helen makes a judgment, adds a buffer for risk, and sends a number.
chapter: A fixed-fee proposal, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: And maybe the number is right.
chapter: A fixed-fee proposal, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Maybe. If it's too high, the client may go elsewhere or push back hard. If it's too low, the firm writes off time at the end and the matter loses money. And because the analysis is so painful, nobody goes back afterwards to learn systematically from the result.
chapter: A fixed-fee proposal, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: Now replay it with the agent.
chapter: A fixed-fee proposal, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Helen opens the pricing tool and describes the matter: acquisition, this sector, roughly this deal size, these jurisdictions, this client. The enrichment layer has already gone through years of the firm's historic time entries and classified them consistently into phases and tasks, even where the original coding was poor. The agent finds the most similar past matters, not just the two Helen remembers but perhaps twenty, and shows her the distribution: typical hours by phase, the range, and the factors that drove the expensive ones.
chapter: A fixed-fee proposal, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: So she sees the spread, not just an average.
chapter: A fixed-fee proposal, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Exactly, and that's crucial for a fixed fee. The agent proposes a budget by phase with a suggested price, and explains it. These matters, these phases, this adjustment for the extra jurisdiction. Helen can change any assumption. She might know something the data doesn't, like this client's habit of reopening negotiated points. She adjusts, and the agent recalculates.
chapter: A fixed-fee proposal, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: And then?
chapter: A fixed-fee proposal, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: Then the matter runs, and the same system tracks actual effort against the budget phase by phase. If diligence is running hot in week two, Helen gets a warning while there's still time to talk to the client about scope. At the end, the result flows back into the data, so the next estimate is better.
chapter: A fixed-fee proposal, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: That's a learning loop.
chapter: A fixed-fee proposal, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: It's the whole point. Pricing stops being a one-off guess and becomes a system that gets more accurate with every matter. And notice the AI isn't replacing Helen's judgment. It's giving her a much better starting point and an early warning system.
chapter: A fixed-fee proposal, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: What does that mean financially?
chapter: A fixed-fee proposal, step by step

speaker: JAMES
text: For the firm, potentially a lot. Write-offs on fixed fees come straight out of profit. If better budgets reduce overruns even a little across hundreds of matters, the money adds up. That's the value story BigHand needs to prove with design partners, with real numbers rather than our hypothetical.
chapter: A fixed-fee proposal, step by step

speaker: NORA
text: Let's step back. What can other software companies, especially those owned by private equity, learn from BigHand?

speaker: JAMES
text: I'd pull out four lessons. The first is that your data may be your AI strategy. BigHand didn't need to invent a new market. It looked at the data its products already collected and asked what AI could do with it. Many vertical software companies sit on similar data and haven't asked that question.

speaker: NORA
text: Second?

speaker: JAMES
text: Second, start with boring AI. Email routing isn't flashy, but it ships, it's useful, and it gets customers comfortable with AI inside the product. That builds trust for the bigger, riskier features like pricing.

speaker: NORA
text: Third?

speaker: JAMES
text: Third, buy when time matters. BigHand partnered with Ayora first, in May, and then bought it in August. That's a sensible sequence. Test the fit through a partnership, then acquire when you're convinced. Buying a small specialist can be much faster than building from scratch, especially when the market is moving quickly.

speaker: NORA
text: And fourth?

speaker: JAMES
text: Fourth, integration is where acquisitions succeed or fail. Buying the capability is the easy part. Getting it inside the core product, working on customers' real data, with a clean experience and a clear price, is the hard part. Anyone who has integrated acquired software knows this. The companies that do it well set a clear owner, a short timeline and measurable milestones.

speaker: NORA
text: If you were running a hundred-day plan for the Ayora integration, what would be in it?

speaker: JAMES
text: First thirty days: pick the design partner firms, agree the success measures, and map exactly how Ayora's enrichment connects to BigHand's pricing data model. Days thirty to sixty: run enrichment on design partners' historic data and have partners review the results, because if the classification is wrong, nothing built on top will be right. Days sixty to a hundred: put the pricing agent in front of a handful of partners on live proposals, in parallel with their normal process, and measure the gap. At day one hundred, decide the general availability date and the pricing model based on evidence.

speaker: NORA
text: And who owns it?

speaker: JAMES
text: One person, with authority across both teams. Split ownership is the classic way integrations drift.

speaker: NORA
text: Let's talk risks.

speaker: JAMES
text: One, commoditisation by general AI tools. If Microsoft and others build good-enough legal workflows into the office suite, BigHand's lighter products come under pressure. Two, billing model change eroding the timecard data advantage over time. Three, clients expecting lower fees. If seventeen percent of firms expect AI to reduce what clients pay, and that number grows, firms' revenue gets squeezed, and that can squeeze their software budgets. Four, execution: integrating Ayora and migrating to the cloud while running a sixteen-product suite.

speaker: NORA
text: And for the owners?

speaker: JAMES
text: Timing. After six years, a sale process at some point is natural. The AI pricing story needs to show traction in revenue to support the valuation a buyer would pay. So speed of execution over the next twelve to eighteen months matters a lot.

speaker: NORA
text: What should listeners watch?

speaker: JAMES
text: Three things. First, an announcement that the Ayora pricing agent is generally available inside Matter Pricing, ideally with named customers or results. Second, how BigHand prices it: bundled, premium tier, or separate product. Third, whether BigHand publishes an AI governance and data use policy for law firm customers. That would be a sign of maturity.

text: Quick-fire round. Short answers.

speaker: JAMES
text: Go.

speaker: JAMES
text: It started as one. Today it's a law firm workflow, pricing and intelligence company.

speaker: NORA
text: Most valuable asset?

speaker: JAMES
text: Years of time, task and matter data inside thousands of law firms.

speaker: NORA
text: Biggest weakness?

speaker: JAMES
text: A sprawling product suite assembled through acquisitions.

speaker: NORA

text: AI Email Routing. Simple, useful, low risk.

speaker: NORA

speaker: JAMES
text: The Ayora pricing agent inside Matter Pricing and Budgeting.

speaker: NORA
text: Will AI kill the billable hour?

speaker: JAMES
text: Not quickly, but it will keep pushing more work to fixed and capped fees. Which is good for BigHand's pricing products.

speaker: NORA
text: One thing a law firm managing partner should do this quarter?

speaker: JAMES
text: Find out how well you can actually measure what your past matters cost. If you can't, you're pricing AI-era work blind.

speaker: NORA
text: Build or buy for legal AI?

speaker: JAMES
text: Both. BigHand built email routing and timecard analysis, and bought Ayora for pricing. Build where you have the data and the know-how, buy where a specialist is already ahead.

speaker: NORA
text: What would make you more confident in the story?

speaker: JAMES
text: Named customers using the pricing agent on live proposals, and a before-and-after number on budget accuracy.

speaker: NORA
text: What would worry you?

speaker: JAMES
text: A long delay in getting Ayora inside the core product, or firms refusing to let their data be enriched at all.

speaker: NORA
text: One piece of advice for a law firm choosing an AI pricing tool?

speaker: JAMES
text: Test it on your own past matters first. If it can't explain matters you already know the answer to, don't trust it on new ones.

speaker: NORA
text: Who should own pricing inside a law firm?

speaker: JAMES
text: A dedicated pricing team working with the partners, not partners alone. The firms with professional pricing functions will get far more out of these tools.

speaker: NORA
text: And who benefits most if BigHand gets this right?

speaker: JAMES
text: Honestly, clients. Better pricing means fewer surprise bills and more fixed fees they can rely on. Firms benefit through fewer write-offs. And BigHand benefits by becoming the system firms can't price without.

speaker: NORA
text: What's the biggest misconception about legal AI?

speaker: JAMES
text: That it's all about drafting and research. Some of the largest gains are in the business of law: pricing, staffing and knowing what work really costs.

speaker: NORA
text: Last quick one. One word for BigHand's next two years?

speaker: JAMES
text: Prove. Prove the pricing agent, prove the integration, prove the revenue.

speaker: NORA
text: Optimist or pessimist?

speaker: JAMES
text: Optimist. BigHand has the data, the customers and a credible AI thesis. It comes down to execution.

speaker: NORA
text: Let me try a summary. BigHand began as a dictation company in the mid-nineties and grew, through three private equity owners and a string of acquisitions, into a suite of around sixteen products that help law firms manage work, documents, pricing and performance, with about four thousand two hundred customers. The legal market is wrestling with how AI changes the economics of legal work, and with clients pushing for fixed fees, firms need to understand what their work really costs. BigHand's bet is that its data, enriched and fed to an AI pricing agent from the Ayora acquisition, can become the tool firms use to price the AI-era law firm. The challenges are integration, cloud migration and proving the agent works on real data. The prize is a pricing product that firms pay for because it makes their fixed fees profitable.

speaker: JAMES
text: That's it. And the lesson for other software companies is clear. When AI changes your customers' business model, the most valuable thing you can sell them is help with their economics, not just their productivity.
